newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-IRISH PUNT UP FOR REALIGNMENT?-BY H.NAUMER.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-IRISH PUNT UP FOR REALIGNMENT?-BY H.NAUMER.

text.p: By Hans-Joerg Naumer, Economist in Currency and Bond Market Research at Sociiti Ginirale in Frankfurt

The majority of the currencies that are potential participants in monetary union stand at rates not far removed from their ERM central rates, yet the Irish punt is about 10 percent above its mark parity rate.
Some market observers have already speculated that a realignment of the Irish currency is possible.

The motivation is understandable -- if there should be an early announcement on the method by which the currency conversion rates for participating currencies will be set on E-Day and the central rates are set at the parity levels, then the difference between the cash market price and the central rate could be exploited by speculators.
However this would only be the case if there was no need to factor in a revaluation of punts, which would close this gap.
The realignment expected by some commentators is supported by two main arguments.

1. A realignment would increase the Irish central bank's room to act. Given unchanged fluctuation bands of +/- 15 percent, it could implement interest rate rises without risking a further appreciation in the currency and a violation of the upper boundary of the band.

2. The exchange rate criterion as laid down in article 109j would not be breached. This criterion calls for a member state to have "respected the normal fluctuation margins provided for by the Exchange Rate Mechanism".
It remains to be seen to what extent this argumentation is valid. It fails to take account of a whole series of points.

1. A realignment would no doubt make it easier to stay within the "normal fluctuation bands" from today's perspective, but would also pose a question as to whether the necessary sustainability had been acheived.

The Treaty actually calls for the fluctuation bands to be respected for more than two years in advance of the decision on the participants, which is due to take place next spring. A realignment would make very clear that the current central rate was inadequate. On the other hand, one can question to what extent the exchange rate criterion has any importance at all since the old EMS was abandoned. This question is not uncontroversial.
2. A change in the central rate would be more or less the same as taking a pre-emptive decision on the conversion rates.

Sociiti Ginirale Frankfurt is generally of the view that an announcement on how the conversion rates will be established will be made by spring of next year at the latest. But the time does not yet seem to be ripe for this, particularly as a realignment for Ireland would be an irreversible solo run. The definition of the conversion rates is a decision of the European Council. The council will not meet again until the end of October at the earliest to sign the Amsterdam Treaty.
3. Punt and sterling are closely linked.

In recent times there were only short-term disturbances in the parallel movements of the two currencies, which were triggered by speculation that rates could be fixed at the current central rates. While the Irish punt from time to time depreciated to its central rate, sterling was not affected by this as it is a clear opt-out currency. But this has changed nothing in the historically high level of correlation between the two currencies.

The close link between the two currencies is probably the strongest argument against a realignment as one cannot assume that sterling will remain at its current level nor that it will enter European monetary union at a similarly high rate, albeit at a later date. The shock of sterling's forced exit from the ERM after it joined at an ambitiously high rate has left a lasting impact and no one can be interested in Britain rejoining the single currency at an excessively high rate. If the central rate of the punt were increased this would in effect isolate sterling. While sterling has further room for depreciation and is likely to join EMU at a rate below the current level, the punt would be "frozen" at a higher level.

But this "decoupling" of exchange rates is dangerous because the two states' economies are closely linked. In addition one must assume that the current rates are being influenced by the "EMU factor" and not just by fundamental factors. Sterling has benefited against the mark as "safe haven" from the euro and increased in the slipstream of the punt.

A higher central rate, which may become the irreversible conversion rate, therefore harbours the danger that Ireland's currency will be overvalued when it goes into the single currency. This is dangerous due to Ireland's close economic links with the EU and the United Kingdom. Some 72.9 percent of Ireland's exports go to the EU and 55.9 percent of imports come from the EU. Some 25.5 percent of Ireland's exports go to the United Kingdom while imports from the UK account for 35.5 percent of total imports. This also becomes evident in the development of the trade-weighted exchange rate of sterling and punt. Basing the rate calculated by the Bank of England at the start of 1996 at 100, one sees that sterling appreciated to 126.7147 on a trade-weighted basis while the punt is only just above the original index level, at 100.71. This clearly shows Ireland's close link as a "small country" to the main island: the appreciation by both sterling and the punt against the mark meant that the impact on the trade-weighted index could be prevented.

Seen overall, a realignment therefore appears improbable. Speculating that the Irish punt will depreciate in the direction of its central rate to date can make sense. But one should take into account that such a strategy depends on a punctual start of monetary union with Ireland as a member and that one cannot be entirely sure the conversion rates will be fixed at the central rates. One possible alternative would be to fix the conversion rates at the average rates.
